_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Getting children with disabilities into ordinary schools, with trained teachers, ramps and assistive devices such as glasses or hearing aids, clearly helps them learn and stay in school. Inclusive education works better than separate special schools, and the main obstacle is money and political will, not uncertainty about what works.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

what_the_sources_show._note: What the primary sources actually support, and which sources.

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.

reader_with_a_decision: Education ministry planners, donor agency and NGO programme officers in low- and middle-income countries. They decide which disability-education interventions to fund or scale (teacher training, inclusive-school conversion, special or resource units, assistive technology, community-based or parent-focused programmes, cash transfers) and whether the evidence justifies the spend.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Rigorous comparative studies in low- and middle-income countries consistently show that these programmes improve enrolment, attendance and learning for children with disabilities. Reviews rate that evidence moderate or high certainty, and they identify a clear ranking of programme types that matches the common belief. If so, there is no gap between belief and evidence to report.

kill_condition_tested._note: Filled in AFTER going to look, by whoever looked.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Programmes or interventions in low- and middle-income countries aimed at improving educational outcomes (access, enrolment, attendance, retention, completion, learning or academic achievement, and transition) for children and young people with physical, sensory, intellectual, developmental or psychosocial disabilities. It also covers what the evidence says about which types of intervention perform comparatively better.

out.what: Effectiveness of disability-education programmes in high-income countries
out.why: The question is restricted to low- and middle-income settings, where school systems, resources and evidence bases differ substantially.

out.what: How many children with disabilities are out of school or the size of the education gap
out.why: That is a prevalence and description question, not a question about whether interventions work.

out.what: Health, rehabilitation or functional outcomes of interventions (e.g., mobility, vision correction itself)
out.why: Only educational outcomes are in scope; health gains are relevant only insofar as they translate into educational outcomes.

out.what: Whether inclusive education is a human-rights obligation
out.why: That is a normative and legal question; this page addresses empirical effectiveness.

out.what: Detailed cost-effectiveness or budget comparisons across programmes
out.why: Cost data are rarely reported alongside effects. The page will note cost evidence only where it is directly reported, not build an economic analysis.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Quantitative effect estimates on educational outcomes (enrolment, attendance, dropout, completion, test scores or learning assessments) for children and young people with disabilities. These come from randomised trials and quasi-experimental studies with comparison groups in low- and middle-income countries, including sample sizes, effect sizes and how long outcomes were followed.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty or quality ratings assigned by systematic reviews or evidence panels (e.g., GRADE ratings of very low, low, moderate or high certainty, or risk-of-bias judgements) on whether each intervention type improves educational outcomes. It also includes those reviewers' stated conclusions about which types have the strongest or weakest support.
